summary: Defines MIB objects for managing network interfaces based on IEEE 802.12. Network management tools use them to read status and counters from such interfaces.

eli5.summary: It is a set of gauges that lets a manager check on a certain kind of network port from far away.

questions: what is demand priority access method
subtitle: SNMP objects for configuring and counting traffic on 100VG-AnyLAN (IEEE 802.12) network interfaces.

tldr.problem: Network management stations had no standard way to read the status, settings and traffic counters of an interface that uses the IEEE 802.12 Demand Priority medium.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DOT12-IF-MIB module, with a configuration table and a statistics table indexed by ifIndex, and explains how the generic interface objects apply to an 802.12 interface.
tldr.outcome: Managers can open or close the interface, see whether training succeeded, and count high and normal priority traffic and error types. The RFC says it discusses no security issues.

today: RFC 2020 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1996, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says to consult the current IEEE 802.12 standard for newer field definitions.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2020 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing network interfaces based on IEEE 802.12. A MIB is a collection of managed objects in a virtual information store, written in the Structure of Management Information (SMI), a subset of ASN.1. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER.

The definitions are based on IEEE Standard 802.12-1995, Clause 13 (layer management) and Annex C (GDMO specifications for Demand Priority managed objects). Attributes that already exist in the Internet-standard MIB or in the Interfaces Group evolution (octet counts, the MAC address, multicast information) are not defined a second time.
sections.eli5: It is a list of gauges and switches for one kind of network port. Things other lists already cover are not repeated.

sections.title: Where the Module Sits
sections.content:
IEEE 802.12 media are identified by one ifType value, ieee80212(55). The module itself is dot12MIB, placed at { transmission 45 }. IANA maintains the IANAifType textual convention that defines ifType values.

The module has two tables, both indexed by ifIndex: dot12ConfigTable for configuration and status, and dot12StatTable for statistics. A conformance section defines two mandatory groups, dot12ConfigGroup and dot12StatsGroup.

For the old interface group (before RFC 1573) the relationship between an 802.12 interface and an interface is one-to-one, so the ifIndex value identifies the matching instances directly.
sections.eli5: Each port gets one row in a settings table and one row in a counting table, and the port number is the key to find both rows.

sections.title: Fitting With the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
An agent that implements this module must support the ifGeneralGroup, ifStackGroup, ifHCPacketGroup and ifRcvAddressGroup of RFC 1573. The RFC then clarifies how several generic objects apply to 802.12.

  • ifSpeed is 100,000,000 and ifHighSpeed is 100 for current implementations.
  • ifMtu is 1500 when dot12CurrentFramingType is frameType88023, and 4464 when it is frameType88025.
  • ifAdminStatus and dot12Commands are linked: setting one to up/open or down/close sets the other, while reset does not change ifAdminStatus.
  • ifOperStatus is up only when dot12Status is opened; it is down for closed, opening, openFailure and linkFailure.
  • The medium has no virtual circuits, and no tests are defined, so ifTestTable is not required.

MAC addresses are always given in canonical order, even when the interface uses token ring framing.

An 802.12 interface uses Ethernet or token ring frame formats but not their media access protocols. So an agent should not implement RFC 1643, RFC 1650 or RFC 1748 for it. When token ring framing and source routing are in use, it should implement RFC 1749.
sections.eli5: The new gauges only add what the general network-port gauges cannot say. For the rest, the general ones are used with a few notes on how to read them for this port type.

sections.title: Master Mode and Priority Counters
sections.content:
In an 802.12 network, master devices (repeaters or other active controllers such as switches) decide when requesting end nodes may transmit. Devices that do not control the network, such as end nodes or passive switches, operate in slave mode. The dot12ControlMode object (masterMode, slaveMode or learn) reports and configures this. The value learn is returned while an interface autosenses its mode, and changing the object makes the interface retrain.

The statistics are split by priority. The MIB has no normal priority transmit counters, because they can be computed from other counters. The RFC gives the formulas, for example that normal priority octets transmitted equal ifOutOctets minus dot12OutHighPriorityOctets. Normal priority receive counters are provided because they include errored frames, while the ifIn* counters do not.

Error counters separate causes: dot12InIPMErrors counts frames carrying an invalid packet marker added by a repeater (problems with remote cables), while dot12InDataErrors points at problems with the cable directly attached. Each octet counter has a 32-bit and a 64-bit (HC) version, because the 32-bit one rolls over very quickly.
sections.eli5: One device acts like a traffic cop deciding whose turn it is to talk. The counters tell you how many urgent and ordinary messages went by, and where the broken ones were damaged.

sections.title: Training and Link Status
sections.content:
Before an interface can carry traffic it goes through training. The dot12Status object reports where it is: opened, closed, opening, openFailure or linkFailure. Training starts when dot12Commands is set to open (or ifAdminStatus to up) while the status is closed. The end node sends Training_Up to the master and initially goes to linkFailure; when the master answers Training_Down the status becomes opening and training packets are exchanged.

Success requires 24 consecutive error-free packets and acceptable configuration bits, giving opened. If the 24 packets are not passed the result is linkFailure; if they are passed but the configuration bits show a problem, it is openFailure, and dot12LastTrainingConfig holds the bits to diagnose it. After a failure the process restarts after MAC_Retraining_Delay_Timer seconds.

The dot12Commands values are noOp, open, reset and close. Closing stops all transmit and receive actions; a reset retrains the interface and counters keep their values.
sections.eli5: Before two devices can talk, they run a practice round. If they get 24 practice messages through without a mistake, the link is ready. If not, they wait and try again.

sections.title: Training Frames
sections.content:
Training frames are special MAC frames used only while a link starts up. They are built by the device at the lower end of the link, the slave. The frame holds a destination address (six octets, always null), a source address (six octets), a requested configuration (2 octets), an allowed configuration (2 octets), data (594 to 675 octets) and a frame check sequence (4 octets). An end node must use its own source address to pass training, while a repeater may use a null one.

The slave states what it wants in the requested configuration: a 3-bit protocol version, the framing type (00 for 802.3, 01 for 802.5, 11 for either), the address mode (00 single address, 01 promiscuous) and whether the initiator is an end node (0) or a repeater (1). The master answers in the allowed configuration, adding flags for a duplicate address, an incompatible configuration, and access refused for security restrictions.

The first 55 octets of the data field may carry vendor-specific information and the rest are zero. The length of the frame plus the 24-frame rule ensures marginal links do not complete training. The RFC says to consult the current IEEE standard for the up to date field definitions.
sections.eli5: A training frame is a form the new device fills out saying how it wants to connect. The controller writes back whether that is allowed and why not if it is not.

sections.title: Security and Mapping to IEEE Objects
sections.content:
The RFC includes a table mapping every managed object defined for oEndNode in the IEEE 802.12 standard to an SNMP object. Most map to dot12 objects or to IF-MIB objects; aMediaType is marked as not yet mapped. For example, acOpen, acClose and acInitializeMAC map to the open, close and reset values of dot12Commands.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Write access to some objects can open, close or reset an interface, but the compliance statement lets implementations make dot12DesiredFramingType, dot12DesiredPromiscStatus, dot12Commands and dot12ControlMode read-only.
sections.eli5: There is a conversion chart between the official standard's names and the new gauge names. The document does not say anything about safety.

items.label: closed
items.desc: MAC disabled by setting dot12Commands to close.

items.label: opening
items.desc: MAC is in training; training signals have been received.

items.label: openFailure
items.desc: 24 error-free packets passed, but the training configuration bits show a problem.

items.label: linkFailure
items.desc: Training signals not received, or 24 error-free packets not passed.

items.title: DA and SA
items.text: Six octets each. The destination is always null.

items.title: Req Config
items.text: 2 octets: what the slave asks for.

items.title: Data
items.text: 594 to 675 octets; the first 55 may be vendor specific.
